# Progressive Pomodoro (ProgPomo)

Free adaptive focus timer PWA based on the Progressive Pomodoro technique. Start with a 2-minute warm-up, rate each session, and build longer deep-work sessions over time. No ads, no accounts, works offline.

- App: https://effectforward.github.io/Progressive-Pomodoro/

- Rating system: https://effectforward.github.io/Progressive-Pomodoro/progressive-pomodoro-rating-system.html
- Classic vs progressive: https://effectforward.github.io/Progressive-Pomodoro/progressive-pomodoro-vs-classic.html
- About: https://effectforward.github.io/Progressive-Pomodoro/about.html

## What is the Progressive Pomodoro technique?

The Progressive Pomodoro technique is a variation of the classic Pomodoro method, built on one simple idea: focus is trainable. Where a classic timer locks you into a fixed 25-minute session every single time, the progressive version starts you short and grows your sessions as your focus improves.

You begin with a gentle 2-minute warm-up. After each session you rate how it went. Your timer takes that rating and adjusts your next session length, so over time it drifts toward the longest session you can actually sustain.

The technique was created by Mike Rapadas. It applies progressive overload, the same training principle used in fitness, to deep work. Instead of demanding an hour of focus on day one, you build it session by session.

## How the rating system works

After each focus session the timer asks how it went. You pick a rating and the timer suggests your next session length.

- Flow: you were fully absorbed. The timer adds the most time to your next session and skips the break.
- Focused: it went well. The timer adds a good amount to your next session and offers a break.
- Fine: a solid, normal session. The timer still grows the next session, just by a smaller amount.
- Distracted: it was a struggle. The timer shortens the next session so you can recover, down to a 2-minute minimum.

Ratings are suggestions, not orders. The timer suggests a new length and you confirm it, so you stay in control. After a normal session the timer offers a break using your short break setting, which is 5 minutes by default. A Flow rating skips the break entirely.

The adjustments are small on purpose. A strong rating adds a few minutes, a rough rating subtracts a few. That gradual drift is what makes the method sustainable.

## Progressive Pomodoro vs classic Pomodoro

The classic Pomodoro method, created by Francesco Cirillo, uses fixed intervals: 25 minutes of work, 5 minutes of rest, repeated in blocks of four. It is simple and predictable.

The progressive version changes the session length itself: it grows with your focus, starts with a 2-minute warm-up, shortens after a bad day, and grows after a great day. Use classic Pomodoro if you focus well in fixed blocks. Use the progressive version if your focus varies, if 25 minutes feels wrong, or if you want to deliberately build longer deep-work sessions.

## Features

- Adaptive focus timer with a session rating system
- 2-minute warm-up start
- Task management
- Session history
- Built-in binaural beats (headphones required)
- Works offline, installable PWA
- No accounts, no ads, no trackers
- All data stored in the browser's local storage
- Open source under GPLv3

## FAQ

What is the Progressive Pomodoro technique?
A variation of the classic Pomodoro method where session lengths grow as your focus improves. You start short, rate how well each session went, and your timer gradually builds toward longer, deeper work sessions.

How does the timer adapt to my focus?
After each session you rate your focus. Flow and Focused increase your next session length, Fine grows it a little, and Distracted shortens it. Over time the timer drifts toward the session length that matches your real focus.

Is Progressive Pomodoro free?
Yes. ProgPomo is completely free, open source under GPLv3, and has no accounts, ads, or sign-up. All your data stays in your browser's local storage.

Does it work offline?
Yes. ProgPomo is a progressive web app. Once loaded, it works offline and can be installed to your home screen on desktop and mobile.

What are binaural beats and do I need headphones?
Binaural beats play a slightly different frequency in each ear, and your brain perceives the difference as a beat. Headphones are required, because each ear must hear its own tone for the effect to work.
